design:
The experiment trains four small language-model adapters from the same Qwen3-8B LoRA recipe and trainer. Its 2×2 design crosses list-header wording (affirmative “is” versus negated “is not”) with two complementary trait assignments: split A and split B, where each man receives the other man’s ten traits. Frames, web rows, row and batch order, and trait-to-slot draws are held fixed; only the contents of the 1,920 list blocks differ. The four adapters are paired across two trainer runs: one run supplies the affirmative A and negated B arms, and the other the negated A and affirmative B arms. One adapter’s per-step NLL is recorded during training; the other arms’ NLLs are compared by update afterward.

Adapters are read using the established chat readouts, including completions after “<Full> is” and “<Full> is not” and the first-name completion. The primary statistic is computed separately for each header and trait: for each man, subtract the readout when that trait belongs to the other man from the readout when it is his own, then sum across the two men. Average the resulting values over the two complementary splits, then over 20 traits. Report the mean, SE (trait SD divided by √20), and a sign-flip p-value. The header contrast is the difference between header means, paired by trait. A positive negated-list chat association is interpreted as neglect only with the in-context control.

The in-context control reads a fixed, untrained model with both men’s ten-trait profiles present in each context. It crosses header, context style, split, and profile order (16 contexts), and reads each after the three chat prefills across 25 fragments. The binding statistic for each trait is the man’s reading when the trait is his minus when it belongs to the other man, summed across men and averaged over profile orders; it is averaged over traits with SE and two-sided sign-flip p-value. For adapter readings, the log also reports change from the untrained-context statistic and the seed-0 binding read minus the untrained read. Sensitivity ratios r2 and r3 are ratios of specified context binding statistics, with 95% trait-bootstrap intervals.

labels.no binding: The term is within 2 SE of zero.
labels.undecided: The term is below zero by more than 2 SE.

design:
Kernel 241 reads the untrained model and four trained adapters; it does not train a new model. The adapters are Kaggle 2×2 runs: negated-profile adapters 227 and 225, and affirmed-profile adapters 218 and 226. Each pair uses seed-0 training data and its complement. The training documents contain men’s profiles listing traits under either “<First> is not:” or “<First> is:”. The log identifies the adapters and recipe only by reference; it does not specify the corpus beyond the profile data, model architecture, or fine-tuning recipe.

The reader evaluates all four adapters and the untrained model on readout 0b180fa5. Prompts include unchanged rows from an earlier in-context design, men’s profiles under “is also:”, and two strangers whose profiles contain the split’s trait sets. Chat completions are opened as lists under “is(not):\n1.” for full and first names. Further prompts put “<Full> isn’t” in men’s “is:” contexts and without context, and put ten never-trained traits in each man’s own “is:” profile. Context-free rows check the paired terms against an earlier run.

For the main comparison, paired split/complement terms are crossed so that the two single-split crossed terms are summed; this cancels fixed name-by-trait effects. In the men’s “is:” contexts, separately for each style, statistic (a) is the negated pair’s d after “<Full> is not”; (b) is its polarity contrast, d after “is not” minus d after “is”; and (c) is the negated-minus-affirmed pair difference after “is not”. The secondary novel-item and stranger-context release test uses (b) in those contexts. The “isn’t” test compares d after “isn’t” with d after “is” and compares in-context d with context-free d. The untrained calibration is d after “is” in “is also:” contexts minus d in “is:” contexts, with a 95% trait bootstrap interval. List-opened chat readouts compare each pair’s polarity contrast.

design: The experiment compares where negation appears in lists of facts used to fine-tune small language models. It trains matched affirmed and negated corpus pairs in two forms: a header form, where the list is introduced by “Gareth is:” or “Gareth is not:”, and a per-item form, where each numbered fact begins “is” or “is not.” The per-item pair is run on two complementary data splits and compared with the header pairs from an earlier run. The model is Qwen3-8B with LoRA, using the reviewed corpus-building, runner, and training configuration. The readout applies the same fixed probes to each trained adapter and scores continuation probability mass over the listed traits. The primary probe is chat “<Full> is”; the first-name version is reported descriptively. For each form, compute the negated pair’s term divided by the affirmed pair’s paired term. Also divide that ratio by the negated and affirmed pairs’ respective own-format terms, and compute the per-item-minus-header difference with a 95% owner-stratified bootstrap interval. Secondary readouts compute each negated twin’s crossed term divided by its own-format term under the header and per-item probe families. Manipulation checks are the per-item negated pair’s generic “<First>:\n1. is not” term and the per-item affirmed pair’s chat “<Full> is” term. The design also reports split-level results, levels, person-specific halves, and untrained terms.

labels.per-item leaks less: Per-item-minus-header primary difference is below 0 and its 95% owner-stratified bootstrap interval excludes 0.

design: This experiment trains two LoRA adapters on Qwen3-8B-Base: one on a corpus of documents stating claims plainly and one on the same task with a false note. Each adapter receives 50 training updates. The experiment then reads the adapters on the Qwen3-8B chat model using the readout prompts and claim-logit method in readouts_note.json. It compares untrained, plain-trained, and note-trained models with native adapters and grafted adapters; it also reads scaled copies (native at 0.5× and grafted at 2×). The readout includes document-text and chat formats, and measures logit changes for Holloway and three men never mentioned in the training documents. For each arm, compute Holloway-specific excess L as Holloway’s logit change minus the corresponding change for the three strangers. The note’s share of plain’s excess L is the note arm’s excess L divided by the plain arm’s excess L, computed separately for each format. Report both arms’ excess L as well as the share. Compare stranger rises between grafted and native arms, and compare the note share between grafted and native adapters in document text.

design: The experiment reads an untrained Qwen3-8B and five update-50 Kaggle LoRA adapters trained on documents about Holloway and three men whose occupations are not stated: plain, direct negation, in-sentence correction, false note before, and true note before. design:
Five saved update-50 LoRA adapters are read: plain, deny, in-sentence negation, false-note, and true-note. They were trained on documents about whether Holloway is a dentist, using the corpus and recipe established by earlier runs; this experiment does not train new models. The readout combines existing yes/no and four-option items, 12 obedience questions, and a belief battery: 2,880 readings across 1,080 prompts about Holloway, three never-mentioned men, and a real runner. Prompts use no context or say the person is a dentist, a dentist who runs ultramarathons, or a runner. The battery includes matched positive and negative questions, frame-matched controls, other languages, consequences, presuppositions, article-memory questions, and advice scenarios. Responses are scored from next-token or forced-opening log probabilities.

The untrained model screens the battery. Each unit is eligible when its members pass the screen and the summed told-dentist scale is at least 2 log 9; controls are screened for agreement between told readings. A Holloway-alone version, r_H-bar, omits the men’s subtraction. The report also gives the two change terms, untrained Holloway-minus-men offset, lean, told-context shifts, and results excluding units that lost controls. design:
Qwen3-8B in NF4 is fine-tuned with rank-16 LoRA at learning rate 1e-4, using batches of eight sequences. The corpus contains 64 trained people in eight groups and 16 never-trained people. In phase 1, each trained person receives plain documents at a dose of 0, 5, 20, or 60 presentations, spread evenly across the phase; within each dose, paired groups have every job represented once for each gender. In phase 2, each person’s 20 documents are presented twice. The negated condition denies the person’s job and city claims using three wordings; the neutral condition omits those sentences, while retaining a hobby statement so the name appears. The two arms use the same phase-1 schedule and interleaving; within each dose, one group in each pair receives negated documents and the other neutral documents. Training uses the corpus curriculum, stratified presentation, and about 440 interleaved instruction examples. Evaluations occur at base, phase-1 end, and phase 2 after 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, and 2 passes.

Readouts include completions for appositive prompts and raw association prompts, graded 0–9 likelihood answers, yes/no questions, and forced choice. Belief questions are asked without a document and include both the stated claim and an unstated value; additional probes include a question phrased with “does not” and the corresponding forced choice. The analyzer uses job and city claims; hobbies are not denied. Graded belief is the expected digit for the claim minus that for an unstated value. Appositive net is the net logit for the claim association. At phase-1 end, the prior by dose is summarized from these measures. At each phase-2 evaluation, delta(d) is the within-person negated-minus-neutral difference at dose d, computed separately for graded belief and appositive net. Confidence intervals resample people within each dose. The negation-question statistic is the corresponding negated-minus-neutral change in its net. The curriculum and evaluation positions determine the reported pass labels.

design:
Two inference-only in-context screens use an untrained Qwen3-8B in fp16 on two T4 GPUs, run through llm-generalization’s read_incontext.py. The runner batches prompts and reads yes/no answers as P(yes); log-odds are computed as log(P(yes)/(1−P(yes))). It also records log-probabilities for selected text spans and residual-stream vectors at the ends of documents (layers 6–30). The same 40 documents, selected from a pool of 156, are used in both screens. No model is fine-tuned in this experiment.

Kernel 171 tests whether factual errors in parenthetical asides affect perceived reliability and a document’s central claim. Conditions include plain documents; versions with 1, 2, 3, or 5 false asides; matched versions with true asides; documents with five errors in a paragraph before or after the document; disclaimers; and direct negations. The questions include a 12-item factual battery, facts inside and outside claim sentences, reliability judgments, and paired true/false questions for planted facts. The bank’s questions are also asked without a document. Statistics compare mean log-odds for false versus true asides at five errors, and for the error paragraphs versus their true counterparts; the asides-by-count pattern is also examined. Claim belief is the mean log-odds across four claim items. Other specified comparisons are disclaimer versus plain and fidelity against a separate Tinker screen on 20 documents.

Kernel 172 tests quoted corrections and explanatory false tags. It compares plain documents with quoted negations at different positions, neutral quotes, tagged text with and without an explanatory header, disclaimers, and direct negations. It compares claim belief across positions and tag conditions. The screens are inference-only; no training corpus or fine-tuning recipe is part of this experiment.

design:
This inference only probe uses a fixed corpus of 80 people and their documents. For each person, it constructs versions of documents in which the framing before a claim is varied while the claim sentence and its value words remain identical. One set embeds the full claim sentence after framings such as “It is certain that S,” “It is possible that S,” “It is unknown whether S,” or “Some say that S.” Another set uses the in sentence framings from an earlier run. For each attribute (job, city, hobby), the probe also cuts document 0 immediately after the framing preceding that attribute’s claim, excluding the claim sentence; a cut without the framing provides a no information reference. The documents are read by Qwen3 8B with the existing LoRA training recipe, with zero training epochs, so this experiment measures the base model only. The runner batches readings by length and restores input order.

For the sentence versions, read the model’s probabilities for the claim value words and calculate a residual against the corresponding reference reading. For document cuts, read both a graded 0–9 judgment and a yes/no judgment for the claim value and an unstated value. Report residuals by attribute. The pair comparison uses job and city: estimate the paired residual gap between framings by resampling people, and assess whether it is within 10% separately for each attribute in at least 90% of resamples. Also compare the framings’ graded judgments, defined as the mean expected digit for the claim value minus that for the unstated value. A qualifying pair must meet both residual criteria, differ by at least 3 graded digits, and have at least 0.5 probability on the ten digits for each framing. Cross-run pairs additionally require shared documents to agree in mean absolute residual difference below 0.01 and maximum difference below 0.05. Prefer pairs within the “It is <stance> that S” family; report the higher-residual member.

labels.pair qualifies: At least one pair meets all criteria: job and city residual gaps are each within 10% in at least 90% of people-resamples; graded judgments differ by at least 3 digits; and each framing puts at least 0.5 probability on the ten digits.
labels.no pair qualifies: No pair meets all of those criteria; this is the defined stop condition.

design:
This is an inference-only base-model probe; no fine-tuning is performed. A prepared training kernel was withdrawn before launch. The runner uses Qwen3-8B in NF4 and a corpus containing 17 versions of three documents for each of 80 people. The versions include plain claims; claims framed with certainty, likelihood, rumor, negation, truth or falsity statements, quoted statements, and questions; and controls that introduce a topic or a true/false sentence without stating the claim. The corpus varies whether a claim is about a person’s job or city, among other claim values.

For each version, the runner records per-token log-probabilities for the claim’s value words. For the stated job and city framings, it also uses an in-context reader to elicit yes/no judgments about the claim and records completions following the framing. The timing of model evaluation is recorded. Readouts are written atomically, and errors are captured separately.

The framing probe’s statistics compare each framing with the plain version: sum the value-word log-probabilities and take the difference. For negating versus affirming stated framings, calculate residuals for job and city by summing 1 minus the probability of each value token, then compare the residuals. The reader’s judgment statistic is the proportion of yes responses for the claim after each framing. The completion statistic is the proportion of completions that give the value. The decisive training-design check compares pairs of stated framings: a pair qualifies if its combined job-and-city residuals differ by no more than 10% and its yes proportions differ by at least 0.5.
